plan.factor: Gel alkalinity, i.e. the hydroxide concentration relative to the T-atoms that form the framework (Si, Al, P, Ge, B, etc.)
queries: effect of OH/SiO2 molar ratio alkalinity on zeolite phase selectivity FAU LTA MFI
fluoride versus hydroxide mineralizer high-silica zeolite crystallization beta MFI
plan.why: D0 contains the raw mole fractions of OH and each T-atom, but a random forest can only threshold each column independently; it cannot express the ratio OH/(Si+Al+P+...) that dominates phase selectivity. Alkalinity controls silicate anion speciation (Q^n distribution), dissolution/gelation kinetics, and nucleation rate: high alkalinity favors low-density, small-pore frameworks (LTA, SOD, FAU, CHA) and Failed/dense phases at extremes, while low alkalinity (especially fluoride media) favors high-silica, open frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, STT-type). Because evaluation is on held-out publications, a normalized ratio is far more transferable across papers than absolute OH mole fraction, which scales with how each paper normalizes its gel. This ratio is a genuinely new axis the classifier cannot currently compute from any single column.

descriptor.assumptions: Assumes OH mole fraction is reported as free hydroxide (not total Na2O or OH equivalents bound to OSDA) and that framework T-atoms are correctly enumerated in the sum. It ignores the competing fluoride mineralizer pathway (F- vs OH- speciation) and buffering by cations, and it treats all T-atoms as equally OH-reactive. The small constant only prevents division by zero for OSDA-free fluoride routes where OH may be absent.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases, probability mass should move from high-silica open frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, TON) toward low-silica small-pore/dense frameworks (LTA, FAU, CHA, SOD) and, at both extremes (very high or effectively zero alkalinity), toward Failed.
descriptor.falsification: If phase outcome is invariant across wide ranges of OH/(sum of T-atoms) within fixed OSDA/cation systems, or if the same framework appears across the full descriptor range while sibling descriptors (e.g., H2O/T, F/OH) show no interaction, the alkalinity-ratio hypothesis is falsified for this dataset.
descriptor.formula: OH / (Si + Al + P + Ge + B + Ga + Be + Ti + Zn + Sn + Zr + V + Mg + W + 1e-6)
descriptor.hypothesis: The hydroxide-to-framework-T-atom ratio (gel alkalinity) is a primary control on which framework crystallizes: increasing alkalinity shifts phase selectivity from high-silica, more open frameworks (e.g., MFI, *BEA, MTW, TON) toward low-silica, small-pore, dense or cation-stabilized frameworks (LTA, SOD, FAU, CHA, AEN-type), with extreme values favoring Failed (dissolution of metastable phases or fully dense products).
descriptor.mechanism: OH- concentration controls silicate/aluminate speciation (Q^n connectivity of anions), the rate of T-atom dissolution and gelation, and the supersaturation at which nuclei form. High OH- depolymerizes silicate species and accelerates nucleation of low-density frameworks stabilized by charge-balancing cations, while low OH- (especially with F- mineralizer) slows dissolution and allows high-silica open frameworks whose formation requires more siliceous, less deprotonated building units. Trees with D0 columns can threshold OH or Si separately but cannot express their ratio, and a normalized ratio is scale-invariant across papers, so it should transfer to held-out publications better than absolute mole fractions.

plan.factor: Tetravalent-to-framework-heteroatom ratio in the gel: (Si + Ge) / (Al + P + B + Ga + Zn + Be + 1e-6), i.e. a normalized gel Si/Al-type composition ratio
queries: gel Si/Al ratio effect on zeolite phase selectivity FAU MFI BEA synthesis
Ge content germanosilicate framework phase selectivity ITH IWR synthesis gel
plan.why: The single most classic phase-determining variable after alkalinity is the framework composition ratio Si/Al (and, for aluminophosphates, the Si or P balance). D0 only contains each mole fraction as a separate column, and a tree splitting on one column at a time cannot form Si/Al, so low-silica vs high-silica regimes (FAU/LTA/AEN-type at low Si/Al vs MFI/*BEA/MTW/TON at high Si/Al) and Ge-driven germanosilicate phases cannot be directly resolved. A ratio of tetravalent framework-formers (Si, Ge) to trivalent/other heteroatoms (Al, P, B, Ga, Zn, Be) gives the model direct access to this composition axis, complementing the already-added alkalinity descriptor without repeating it.

descriptor.assumptions: The formula assumes Si and Ge play analogous tetravalent framework roles and that Al, P, B, Ga, Zn, Be are the relevant charge-generating heteroatoms; it ignores Al-P charge-compensated aluminophosphate chemistry, where the ratio is uninformative (P and Al coexist and net framework charge is near zero), and it treats all heteroatoms equally despite different charge states (Al3+/Ga3+ vs Zn2+/Be2+) and different degrees of actual framework incorporation. Gel mole fractions are used as a proxy for framework composition; not all gel heteroatoms incorporate. The 1e-6 constant prevents division by zero for pure-silica, pure-germania, or metal-free gels, producing very large values that trees can split on as a 'no heteroatom' regime.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases from ~1 (1:1 tetravalent:heteroatom) toward tens and hundreds, probability mass should move from low-silica/caged frameworks (FAU, LTA, CHA, AEN, MOR, LEV) and aluminophosphate outcomes to high-silica frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, TON, MEL) and Ge-containing topologies (BEC, UTL); extremely large values (near-pure Si/Ge gels) should increase Failed or dense-phase outcomes. The literature shows concrete crossover points: BEA favored below Si/Al ~50, MTW at 50-120, cristobalite above 120 [4]; BEA→SSZ-31→MFI shifts with gel silica-to-alumina ratio and alkalinity [3]; ERI/LTL-type phase selection flips between Si/Al = 6 and ≥15 gels [2]; piperazine yields different 8MR frameworks (ZSM-4/mordenite vs ZSM-35) as the gel SiO2/Al2O3 ratio varies [7].
descriptor.falsification: If held-out-publication accuracy does not improve (or phase splits do not align with this ratio) relative to D0 alone, or if low-silica frameworks appear systematically at high ratio values and high-silica frameworks at low ratio values, the descriptor is not capturing composition-based phase selection and should be discarded. Also falsified if pure-silica aluminophosphate-type outcomes (AFI, AEL) correlate positively with the ratio despite containing no Si.
descriptor.formula: (Si + Ge) / (Al + P + B + Ga + Zn + Be + 1e-6)
descriptor.hypothesis: The ratio of tetravalent framework-forming T atoms (Si, Ge) to lower-valent or charge-generating heteroatoms (Al, P, B, Ga, Zn, Be) in the gel is a primary phase-determining variable that a tree ensemble cannot form from individual mole-fraction columns. Increasing this ratio should shift selectivity from low-silica, cation-stabilized frameworks (FAU, LTA, CHA, MOR, AEN-type, levyne/ERI-type phases) and aluminophosphate products toward high-silica, hydrophobic frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, TON, MEL) and, at very high values, toward dense silica phases or Failed outcomes (cristobalite/uncharged dense phases). Germanosilicate regimes (high Si+Ge with small heteroatom fractions) should favor Ge-stabilized large-pore frameworks such as ITH, IWR, BEC and UTL.
descriptor.mechanism: Framework composition controls the negative charge density of the crystallizing framework and hence which charge-balancing species (inorganic cations, OSDA, fluoride) can stabilize nucleation. Low T4+/T3+ ratio gels have high framework charge density, requiring high cation/OSDA charge density and favoring small-pore, caged, low-silica frameworks (FAU, LTA, CHA, ERI/AEN families). High T4+/T3+ ratio gels have low charge density, favoring neutral or sparsely charged frameworks directed mainly by the OSDA shape (MFI, *BEA, MTW, TON) or by fluoride/Ge chemistry (BEC, ITH, IWR, UTL). Ge substitutes for Si and expands double-ring units, so Ge contribution at high tetravalent ratio steers toward germanosilicate topologies.

plan.factor: water content of the gel relative to framework T atoms (H2O / total framework T-atom mole fraction, i.e., gel dilution / concentration)
queries: effect of water content H2O/SiO2 ratio on zeolite phase selectivity synthesis
gel dilution crystallization zeolite dense phase impurity concentrated gel
plan.why: Water-to-T-atom ratio (or equivalently H2O/SiO2) is one of the most frequently reported phase-determining gel variables in zeolite synthesis, but it emerges only from combining the H2O column with the T-atom columns, so a tree ensemble splitting on single columns cannot access it. Concentration controls nucleation density and the balance between hydrated cation/OSDA-stabilized open frameworks and dense phases: dilute gels (high H2O/T) lower supersaturation, favor fewer nuclei, larger crystals, and often dense or Failed outcomes, while concentrated gels (low H2O/T) promote rapid nucleation of metastable, small-pore or high-silica open frameworks (e.g., LTA, CHA, MFI) and can trigger impurity/dense-phase competition at extremes. It is largely orthogonal to the two descriptors already present (alkalinity OH/T and the tetravalent/heteroatom ratio), which encode base strength and gel composition but not total system concentration, so it should add independent phase-selective signal that transfers across papers since it is a ratio of normalized mole fractions.

descriptor.assumptions: Assumes total framework T-atom mole fraction is a valid proxy for silica-like solute concentration and that water's role scales inversely with it across aluminosilicate, gallosilicate and aluminophosphate systems; for pure aluminophosphate gels (Si~0) the ratio still reflects dilution but the water/SiO2 interpretation weakens. H2O recorded in the gel normalization may exclude water added in washes/solutions, and the same H2O/T value can correspond to different alkalinities, so the descriptor is not a full replacement for OH/T. Fluoride-media rules (e.g., water/Si ~15 thresholds) may not transfer to OH- media.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases (more dilute gels): selectivity should move from open OSDA-rich frameworks (*BEA, MWW, CHA, BEC) toward denser large-pore silicas (MTW/ITQ-4-type, TON) and eventually to Failed/amorphous at very high values. As the descriptor decreases (concentrated gels): small-pore and metastable frameworks (LTA, CHA, MFI, FER) and impurity/dense-phase competition should become more likely.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out recipes show no systematic split on water_per_tatom_dilution across phase labels, or if the same framework crystallizes across the full descriptor range while other phases vary independently of it (i.e., water/T carries no feature importance or directions opposite to the hypothesis), the hypothesis is contradicted.
descriptor.formula: H2O / (Si + Al + P + Ge + B + Ga + Be + Ti + Zn + Sn + Zr + V + Mg + W + 1e-6)
descriptor.hypothesis: The water-to-framework-T-atom ratio (gel dilution) is a phase-determining variable that a tree ensemble cannot access from single columns. Increasing dilution raises the water/Si ratio and thereby shifts phase selectivity: concentrated gels (low H2O/T) favor less dense, OSDA-occluding open frameworks (e.g., *BEA/Beta over ITQ-4/MTW-type), promote rapid nucleation of small-pore and metastable frameworks (MFI, CHA, LTA), and at extreme concentration cause incomplete dissolution and impurities; dilute gels (high H2O/T) lower supersaturation, slow crystallization, favor the denser competing phase (e.g., ITQ-4/ZSM-12 over Beta) and, at excessive values, yield amorphous or Failed products.
descriptor.mechanism: Water sets the concentration of dissolved silicate/aluminate and OSDA species, hence the supersaturation and nucleation density. At low water/T, high supersaturation and strong ion-pairing/cation hydration favor nucleation of open, OSDA- or cation-stabilized frameworks and lower the Al threshold at which the less dense phase appears (Al addition and water decrease act in the same direction on selectivity). At high water/T, lower supersaturation favors slower growth of the thermodynamically denser phase, reduces mineralizer OH- activity (raising effective pH sensitivity), and beyond an optimum dilution the medium loses ion-transport capability and crystallinity collapses to amorphous material.
